clocks.text: Decides after the session end using closes up to that day; fills at the next session-end mid plus or minus 0.05%.

Weekly strategies: decide after the last scheduled session end of each ISO week (a holiday is known in advance; an unannounced closure gives a 'late' decision on the next week's first session) and fill at the next session end; they hold in between.
Long-hold strategies: decide on the first session of each month (the champion-review session) and fill at the next session end; no exit date.
The main book's own orders, filled at the 22:50 quote of the fill session (buy at the ask, sell at the bid); modelled when no quote was recorded.
Diagnostic only: fills at the same close the signal was computed from. Not executable by hand; never champion.
Probe: decides from the recorded tape up to 22:38 and fills at that session's close. Live recorded sessions only.
Probes: decide and exit within one session from the recorded tape; a flat same-day round trip pays no transaction tax.

timetable.text: Finalised history for Allianz, SAP and Eni compared with the stored close; targeted history for names missed.
90-second quote windows from the live stream (stream mode only).
Partial tape pass, only in sleepy mode.
Quote window for the hand-execution shadow and spread measurement.
Main tape pass, one request every 1.5 s (about 3 minutes).
The session is settled if at least 95% of tradable names have a close.

Names still missing take the finalised history point if there is one. With 95% of the closes the session is settled (flagged partial if names are missing); below that it waits for the next morning's finalised history. No session is ever settled without closes.
One drills batch of up to 10 minutes in a low-priority subprocess.
The tape for a session can still be recorded until 06:55 the next morning.
History for all 111 items; verifies the week's closes.

text: €1.00 per paper order (costs.json item tr_fee_best_price); a kept position sends no order.
Fills at the session-end mid ± 0.05% (assumed; tr_spread_third_party). Measured spreads re-price live fills beside the books, never instead.

Transaction tax on net purchases per book, stock and session: Italy 0.4% (it_ftt_rate_2026, it_ftt_otc_definition), France 0.4% (fr_ftt_rate), Spain 0.2% (es_ftt). The buyer pays; a flat same-day round trip pays none (it_ftt_intraday_net).

Whole shares; minimum ticket €1,000; €10,000 of paper per book. Cash earns 0% (Trade Republic's rate and terms could not be verified). No dividend is credited: daily books exit before known ex-dates, weekly books do not enter into one, long-hold books hold through them (the understatement is shown).
Weekly and long-hold books skip a name whose price is above the ticket at the decision (prices known at the decision); daily books cancel at the fill, as in season 1.

Round-trip cost c(T) = 2 × €1 / T + 2 × half-spread + tax. Learner books enter only when the forecast is at least k × c(T); the entry test ignores the 26% tax, which scales a gain without changing its sign.
26% Italian tax on realised gains, withheld at each paper sale (see Tax). Not modelled: Belgian, Finnish and Luxembourg transfer taxes (not checked), stamp duty or IVAFE (unresolved).

champion_rule.text: Season 3: the main book follows one strategy fixed in advance, W4 (WRIDGE250-ALL-BAND), chosen by the owner on 30 Sep 2026 for a higher risk profile, after its 2016–2026 history was known. There is no monthly champion review. W4 decides after the last session of each week and fills at the next session end. If W4's own paper book falls below its stop band (possible only after 60 live sessions), the main book holds cash until the flag clears. The 54 configurations tried so far are counted in the tests.

wording.headline: {m} of 10 pre-registered criteria met.
wording.too_early: {n} of 250 live sessions. No verdict is possible before about {date} at the earliest. Until then the scorecard can only fail, not pass.
wording.always: This scorecard was fixed on {registered_on} (season {s}, hash {sha8}), before any live result existed. It checks whether the paper record passed tests chosen in advance. Money results are after the 26% Italian tax on gains; no dividends are credited and cash earns 0%. Paper fills at the L&S session-end mid are easier than real ones, and backtests use today's index members. A few months of paper trading can confirm fills and costs, not an edge. Meeting every criterion would not show that results will continue, and it is not a recommendation. The lab trades pretend money only. The lab places no real orders and recommends none.
wording.history_failed: At registration the history did not pass {list}. In this season the scorecard cannot reach 10 of 10. The lab keeps trading on paper to measure costs, spreads, taxes and live behaviour. A new season would restart the live clock and raise the bar.
wording.all_met: All 10 criteria are met by the paper record since {live_start}. This is a statistical statement about past paper trades under the rules registered on {date}; it does not say the model will make money, and it is not advice. The lab places no real orders and recommends none.
wording.expectation: The research read for this lab expects a small edge before costs and a result near zero or below after retail costs and tax; fewer than 1% of Taiwanese day traders reliably made money after fees [d13]. Weekly and long-hold strategies trade less, but their history is flattered by today's index members, and the long-hold books receive no dividends. That outcome would itself be the finding.

evidence.title: Short-term reversal in Europe, net of costs · de Groot, Huij & Zhou, 2012
evidence.claim: Among the 100 largest European stocks (1995–2009), a daily-rebalanced one-week reversal long-short earned 96.5 bps/week gross but −47.7 bps/week after institutional trading costs; only a turnover-cutting 'smart' rule left +21.6 bps/week net (t = 2.3).

evidence.title: Bid-ask bounce and decay in daily reversal · Nagel, 2012
evidence.claim: In US stocks (1998–2010) a 1–5 day reversal strategy earned 0.30% per day on closing trade prices but only 0.18% per day on quote midpoints, so a large part of the measured profit was bid-ask bounce.

evidence.title: Conditioning reversal on market state · Nagel, 2012
evidence.claim: Daily reversal returns are strongly predictable from the VIX: a one-point rise in normalised VIX adds 0.22 percentage points to the daily reversal return.

evidence.title: Overnight vs intraday returns · Lou, Polk & Skouras, 2019
evidence.claim: In US stocks (1993–2013) the one-month reversal shows no close-to-close effect, yet its alpha is +0.93%/month overnight and −1.05%/month intraday.

evidence.title: Overnight vs intraday returns in Europe · STOXX (Seegopaul), 2025
evidence.claim: For the iShares Core EURO STOXX 50 ETF (Jan 2016–Oct 2025), close-to-open returns were +12.9% a year and open-to-close returns −4.3% a year.

evidence.title: Time zones: the European open and US order imbalances · Boyarchenko, Larsen & Whelan, 2023 and 2026
evidence.claim: S&P 500 futures earned 3.7% a year in the hour when Europe opens (1998–2020); after bid-ask costs the hour-long strategy's Sharpe fell from 1.1 to −0.5.

evidence.title: International lead-lag across time zones · Lin, Engle & Ito, 1994
evidence.claim: Foreign daytime returns show up in the next domestic opening price, but apart from one post-crash case there were no significant lagged spillovers into the following daytime.

evidence.title: Turn-of-month effect and its disappearance · McConnell & Xu, 2008; Han, Han & Tian, 2025
evidence.claim: Up to January 2006 the four-day turn-of-month window beat other days in most markets, but not in Italy and only weakly in France; later studies report it faded.

evidence.title: Calendar effects under White's Reality Check · Sullivan, Timmermann & White, 2001
evidence.claim: Across 9,452 calendar rules on 100 years of daily Dow data, the best rule had a nominal p-value below 0.002 but a Reality Check p-value of 0.24.

evidence.title: Intraday momentum, first half-hour to last half-hour · Gao, Han, Li & Zhou, 2018
evidence.claim: On S&P 500 ETF data for 1993–2013, the first half-hour return (from the previous close) predicts the last half-hour return.

evidence.title: Intraday momentum in European index futures · Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens, 2021
evidence.claim: Across 8 European index futures, the return from the prior close to 30 minutes before the close predicts the last half-hour.

evidence.title: Transaction costs and turnover · Novy-Marx & Velikov, 2016
evidence.claim: One-month short-run reversal (91% monthly turnover) earned 0.37%/month gross and −1.28%/month net; few high-turnover strategies survive costs.

evidence.title: Retail day-trader performance after fees · Barber, Lee, Liu & Odean, 2014
evidence.claim: Among roughly 450,000 Taiwanese day traders a year (1992–2006), fewer than 1% reliably earned positive abnormal returns after fees.

evidence.title: Deflated Sharpe ratio · Bailey & López de Prado, 2014
evidence.claim: An annualised Sharpe of 2.5 over five years of daily data, picked from 100 trials with skew −3 and kurtosis 10, has only a 90% chance of a true Sharpe above zero.

evidence.title: Probability of backtest overfitting and cross-validation · Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, 2016
evidence.claim: Combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV) estimates how often the in-sample best configuration falls below the median out of sample.

evidence.title: Multiple testing: the t > 3 hurdle · Harvey, Liu & Zhu, 2016
evidence.claim: With at least 316 published factors, a new factor should clear a t-statistic of about 3.0, not 2.0.

evidence.title: Machine learning at daily frequency and its post-2010 decay · Krauss, Do & Huck, 2017
evidence.claim: ML ensembles on daily S&P 500 constituents earned 0.25%/day after 5 bps per half-turn until 2009; in 2010–2015 every model lost 14–25% a year after costs.

evidence.title: Online learning with forgetting and shrinkage · Chinco, Clark-Joseph & Ye, 2019
evidence.claim: A LASSO re-estimated every minute on a rolling 30-minute window raised out-of-sample R² over a benchmark: estimation with forgetting plus shrinkage.

evidence.title: Momentum · Jegadeesh & Titman, 1993
evidence.claim: Buying the US stocks that rose most over the past 6 months and short-selling those that fell most, then holding for 6 months, earned about 1% a month in 1965–1989 (NYSE and AMEX, before a 0.5% one-way cost test); part of it reversed over the following two years.

evidence.title: 52-week high · George & Hwang, 2004
evidence.claim: US stocks closest to their 52-week high beat those furthest from it by about 0.45% a month in 1963–2001, before trading costs, and the gain did not reverse in the long run.

evidence.title: Trend filter · Faber, 2007
evidence.claim: Holding the S&P 500 only when its month-end price was above its 10-month average returned 10.18% a year against 9.32% for buy-and-hold in 1901–2012 and cut the worst fall from 83.66% to 42.24%; it times a whole index, not single stocks, and excludes taxes and commissions.

evidence.title: Weekly reversal · Lehmann, 1990
evidence.claim: Last week's US losers tended to rise and winners to fall the next week (1962–1986); at 0.40% one-way costs the version built to strip out bid-ask bounce earned roughly zero.

evidence.title: Published rules fade · McLean & Pontiff, 2016
evidence.claim: Across 97 published US stock-return predictors, returns were 26% lower after the original sample period and 58% lower after publication.

text: Every book keeps an Italian tax ledger, as a broker does under the regime amministrato: 26% of each realised gain on shares is withheld from the book's cash at the sale (D.Lgs. 461/97 art. 6 c.9).

Gain = sale proceeds − purchase cost; both €1 fees reduce the gain (TUIR art. 68 c.6). The Italian transaction tax is not deductible (L. 228/2012); the lab does not deduct the French and Spanish ones either (not verified; the cautious side).

A loss becomes a credit against later gains in the same year and the next four (art. 6 c.5), used oldest first; tax already withheld is never refunded. A credit from year Y lapses at the start of the first session of Y + 5.
The Europe ETF (X1) follows the fund rule: the gain is capital income, taxed at 26% with no deductions and not offset by credits; its losses and fees become credits.
Sales in the same session are booked in ISIN order: the lab has no execution times. A real investor who sold the losing position first could pay slightly less tax that evening.
PRE-TAX = the book with the withheld tax added back. AFTER-TAX = the book less the tax that selling everything that evening would withhold. Neither deducts the exit fees or spread of that sale.
Today's rules are applied to all of history (the rate was 12.5% before 2012 and 20% from 2012 to 30 June 2014).

not_built: No real-money mode of any kind: no Trade Republic connection, credentials, order routing, broker export or order ticket.
No state that calls the lab fit for real money, no suggested amount, no probability of profit for a next trade.
No notification or briefing line that names a stock or asks for an action.
No labels that rank the 108 shares by attractiveness; the ladder is the paper book's own forecast list.
No tuning UI or API: every change is a code change, a new season and a ledger line.
No same-day or LATE-clock strategy eligible for champion before a new season built on 250 recorded sessions.
No short selling, leverage, options, CFDs or margin; ETFs only as references.
No neural networks, boosted trees or random forests; no numpy in the lab; no LLM calls.
No calendar, technical-rule, news or sentiment features; no VIX scraping.
No stop-losses, take-profits or trims.
No spike replacement that peeks at the next day; no automatic dividend detection in decisions.
No second price vendor, no past-intraday back-fill, no weekend sessions, no parallel fetches, no polling of the 111 names.
The lab itself installs no launchd agent, wake schedule or other system-setting change.
No recomputation of committed live sessions; corrections are appended.
No blended history-plus-live headline figure; demo data is always badged.
No main book that blends families, and no chained return across seasons as a headline.
No crediting of dividends or cash interest in any book; no dividend or interest scraping; no interest overlay on the public site.
No fractional sizing.
No data from My Portfolio (the owner's real portfolio) in clear on the public site: it is published only encrypted and opens with the owner's code.
No analytics, cookies, trackers, comments, newsletters or visitor alerts on the public site; its only outside requests are its fonts (Google Fonts) and chart libraries (jsDelivr).

No automatic creation of GitHub repositories and no credential storage. Each snapshot replaces the previous one as a single commit force-pushed to gh-pages; the lab's own record is append-only (committed sessions are never recomputed).
No 'copy' or 'follow these trades' wording; no performance claims beyond the data.

No forecast, expected return or hurdle for a named stock on the public site. (Season 3: the Trading Lab tab does show the main book's paper positions and next paper orders, next to the paper-money disclaimer.)
No change to season 3's parameters from the UI or the API: every change is a code change, a new season and a ledger line.
No monthly champion review in season 3: the main book follows W4, the owner's fixed choice, until a new season is registered.
